title: Opposite-Coloured Bishops
subtitle: The most drawish endgame — and the most dangerous middlegame.
goals: Hold a draw two pawns down
Place pawns on the colour the enemy bishop can't reach
Know when opposite bishops favour the attacker

steps.say: When each side has one bishop and they travel on different colours, the pieces can never meet — and the usual rules break. In the ENDGAME this is the most drawish material in chess: a single bishop can hold back two or even three pawns forever, because the attacker's bishop can never challenge the blockading square. In the MIDDLEGAME the same fact makes attacks deadly: on the attacking colour, the defender is effectively a piece down.

steps.prompt: You're Black, a pawn down. Set up the blockade that draws!
hints: The pawn stands on a light square and your bishop is dark-squared — you can never attack it. Block the square in FRONT of it instead.
c6 is a dark square: Be5 covers it and the pawn can never pass.

line.say: The blockade. c6 is a dark square, so your bishop controls it forever — and White's light-squared bishop can never challenge you there. The pawn is stopped for good: a draw held by a piece that cannot even touch the thing it is stopping.

rejections.say: Never trade! Once the opposite-coloured bishops leave the board, the extra pawn simply wins. Your bishop's inability to meet his is precisely what saves you.
The king walks while the pawn runs: c6, c7, c8. Blockade with the BISHOP first — the king only helps afterwards.

steps.wrongSay: You cannot attack a light-squared pawn with a dark-squared bishop. Block its path instead.
steps.successSay: Blockade, don't capture. That single idea saves countless 'lost' endgames.

steps.prompt: Now TWO connected passers — still drawable. Find the blockading square!
hints: Your bishop is light-squared, so it can only stop a pawn standing on (or heading to) a light square.
Bd5! One bishop stops both pawns: b6 is covered by the blockade, and c6 is a light square your bishop owns.

line.say: One bishop, two pawns, total blockade. This is the miracle of opposite-coloured bishops: material means almost nothing, the COLOUR of the blockading square means everything. White can shuffle forever and never break through.

rejections.say: Close — but from e6 the bishop doesn't stop the b-pawn's advance, and after b6 the pawns roll. The one square that halts BOTH is d5.
Passive king moves lose the race — the pawns are much faster. The blockade must be set by the bishop, immediately.

steps.wrongSay: One square stops both pawns. It must be a light square your bishop can hold.
steps.successSay: Two connected passers, held by one bishop — opposite bishops in a nutshell.

steps.prompt: Switch sides: you're the attacker now. Put your pawns where the enemy bishop can never touch them!
hints: Your bishop is dark-squared. Enemy dark squares are therefore yours to control — so your PAWNS belong on light squares, where his dark bishop can never attack them.
b4 keeps the pawns on light-square duty and supports the c5 passer.

line.say: Correct: pawns on the colour the enemy bishop cannot attack, and your own bishop covering the squares in front of them. That combination — pawns on one colour, bishop on the other — is how the attacking side actually converts opposite-bishop positions.

rejections.say: Kingside expansion on the wrong wing, and it weakens your king's dark squares — exactly where his bishop lives. When bishops are opposite, put your pawns where his bishop can't go and keep your king off his colour.

steps.wrongSay: His bishop is dark-squared. Which colour should your pawns stand on?
steps.successSay: Drawish for the defender, deadly for the attacker — opposite bishops reward whoever understands the colour complex better.
